turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response: Well, hello, Doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I, uh, I guess I'm here because I just keep messing up these little things, and it's starting to really bother me. I mean, it's not like I'm making huge, life-altering mistakes, but it's these constant, annoying little slip-ups. For instance, just the other day, I was at the senior center—I go there a few times a week, you know, just to stay active and see some folks—and I was signing up for this woodworking class. I was so excited about it, I've always liked working with my hands, but when I wrote down the time for the class, I completely botched it. I wrote down 2:00 PM instead of 10:00 AM. I have no idea why, the paper was right in front of me, but I just didn't pay attention to the details. I showed up four hours late and missed the whole first session! And speaking of woodworking, that's another thing. I was in my garage trying to build this little birdhouse for my yard, just a simple project, right? I measured the board, I swear I looked right at the tape measure, but I must have just skimmed over the little lines, the small print, so to speak, because when I made the cut, it was a hair short. Just enough to ruin the whole piece. It's so frustrating because I know I looked at it, but my brain just sort of skipped the important part. It's like I'm looking right at something, but the details just slide right past me. It's just... it's happening a lot lately, these little careless things.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly describes making careless mistakes and failing to pay attention to details, such as writing down the wrong time for a class and mismeasuring a board because they skipped over the small print.

turns.doctor_question: Have these kinds of careless mistakes and trouble paying attention been present since you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, gosh, yes. You know, it's funny you ask that, because I was actually just going through some old boxes in the attic a few months ago. My late mother, bless her heart, she kept absolutely everything. Every little drawing, every scrap of paper... and she had all my old report cards from back in elementary school. I sat there on this dusty old trunk reading them, and, well, it was like reading about the exact same fellow sitting in front of you right now. 

I mean, my teachers—I remember Mrs. Gable in third grade especially, she had this very neat, looping cursive—they all wrote the exact same kind of notes in the margins year after year. They always said I was a bright boy, you know, that I had a good head on my shoulders and the potential was there, but... well, there was always a "but." 

They wrote that I was constantly forgetting my reading books, just leaving them on my desk at school or leaving them at home when I needed them in class. And my homework? Good grief. It was a miracle if it made it out of my house. I'd lose the papers completely before they ever got turned in. And the other thing they all agreed on, which I suppose makes a lot of sense now, was how I'd just sit there and stare right out the classroom window. I remember there was this big oak tree outside my fourth-grade class, and I'd just watch the leaves or the squirrels, completely zoned out, unless the teacher or someone actually came over and kept me on track. If they didn't physically walk down the aisle, tap my desk, and redirect me, my mind was just... gone, out the window with the birds. So, yes, doctor, it's definitely not a new problem. It's been happening since I was just a little guy in short pants.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly agrees ('Oh, gosh, yes') to the doctor's question about having a history of making careless mistakes.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes a lifelong history of trouble paying attention, noting he would 'completely zone out' in class unless a teacher kept him on track.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient reports constantly forgetting his reading books and losing his homework papers before they could be turned in.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as watching leaves or squirrels outside the classroom window.

turns.doctor_question: Do these attention and forgetfulness problems happen in more than one part of your life, like at home, work, and social activities?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yes, I'd have to say it really does bleed into just about everything, unfortunately. It’s not just one area where I’m dropping the ball. Like I mentioned with the senior center, I actually used to help lead a couple of the DIY workshops there. Nothing too fancy, just basic birdhouses, picture frames, that sort of thing. I really enjoyed it, but... well, I had to step back from doing it. I was getting the materials mixed up, forgetting which tools I told people to bring, or I'd lose the sign-up sheets. It just got too embarrassing, frankly, feeling like I couldn't keep a simple workshop organized. So I had to bow out of leading those, which was a real shame because I liked helping the other folks. 

And then at home, oh boy, my wife, Mary, she’s a saint, she really is. But it’s gotten to the point where she has to double-check absolutely every plan we make. If we’re supposed to go over to our daughter’s house for a Sunday roast, or if there’s a potluck at the center, Mary has to confirm the times and the dates with me, usually more than once. Because if she doesn't, I’ll end up writing it down wrong on the kitchen calendar, or I'll just completely forget we even had something scheduled and I'll be out in the garage covered in sawdust when we're supposed to be leaving. I hate that she feels like she has to manage me, you know? It throws off our family visits, it messes up the center activities... it just feels like I can't be trusted to keep my own schedule straight anywhere I go. So, yes, it's definitely happening at home, at the center, with the family... it's just everywhere.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient describes making careless mistakes, such as getting materials mixed up and writing dates down incorrectly on the calendar.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly mentions feeling unable to keep a simple workshop organized, leading him to step down from leading them.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient reports losing sign-up sheets that were necessary for the workshops he was leading.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient describes forgetting which tools he told people to bring and completely forgetting scheduled family visits and center activities.
